notes.meaning: The Lord tells Moses how to handle deliberate sins against other people. These sins include lying about borrowed goods, cheating a partner, stealing, or finding lost property and lying under oath about it. Even though these crimes harm a neighbor, God treats them as unfaithfulness against Himself because His name was used to tell a lie. Cheating or lying to another person is always a direct offense against God.

When a guilty person feels conviction in his conscience and confesses, he must return everything he took dishonestly. He must also add an extra fifth of the value to compensate the owner for the loss and trouble. This repayment must happen on the very day he admits his guilt, before he presents his offering to God. True repentance requires making right the harm done to others whenever possible.

After making things right with the person he wronged, the offender must bring a flawless ram to the priest as a guilt offering. The priest presents the sacrifice to make atonement, which means making amends to restore the broken relationship with God, and God promises full forgiveness. Paying back the neighbor cannot remove guilt before God, because only the sacrifice can do that. God mercifully pardons even deliberate sins when someone turns away from their wrongdoing and seeks Him.

God gives special instructions directly to the priests about how to carry out their duties at the altar. The evening burnt offering had to be arranged so that it would smolder slowly throughout the entire night. The priests had to watch over the hearth to ensure the fire never went out before morning. This showed the continuous devotion God's people owed Him through every hour of the night.

Every morning, the priest had to wear his sacred linen garments to clear the ashes off the altar and set them nearby. He then changed out of his holy garments into ordinary clothes to carry those ashes outside the camp to a clean place. Even the leftover ashes of God's sacrifice were treated with dignity and care. God's ministers were taught that no task done for His altar was too lowly or dirty to perform.

The fire on the altar had originally come down from heaven and was never allowed to die out. Each morning the priest added fresh firewood, arranged the daily burnt offering on the flame, and burned the fat of peace offerings. This continuous fire showed that the worship of the Lord must never stop. Believers are reminded to keep the flame of prayer and holy love alive in their hearts every day.

The priests are given instructions on how to handle the grain offerings brought by the people. The priest took a handful of fine flour mixed with olive oil, along with all the fragrant frankincense, to burn on the altar. This small portion was called the memorial because it represented the whole gift being given to God. The pleasant scent showed God's delight and acceptance of the worshiper's gift.

The rest of the grain offering belonged to Aaron and his male descendants for their daily food. It had to be baked without yeast and eaten only within the sacred courtyard of the tabernacle because it was most holy. Since the priests dedicated their lives to sacred service, God provided for them directly from His own altar. Anyone or anything that touched these sacred gifts had to be consecrated and treated with deep respect.

When the high priest was anointed into office, he had to bring a grain offering of about two quarts of fine flour. Half of this flour was offered in the morning and half in the evening as a continual practice throughout his ministry. It was cooked with oil on a griddle, kneaded well, broken into pieces, and offered to the Lord. This daily offering reminded the high priest that he also needed God's grace each day.

Whenever a son of Aaron was anointed to succeed him as high priest, he had to follow this same permanent rule. Unlike the grain offerings brought by ordinary Israelites, no part of a priest's own grain offering could ever be eaten by the priests. The entire offering had to go up in smoke upon the altar as a gift completely surrendered to the Lord. Because priests were sinners who could not make atonement for themselves, they could not eat their own sacrifices.

God explains how the priests must handle the sin offering. The animal had to be killed on the north side of the altar, the very same spot where the burnt offering was slain. The officiating priest was commanded to eat the remaining meat in the tabernacle courtyard because this offering was most holy. By eating this meat, the priest symbolically carried the guilt of the people so that it was removed before God.

The meat and blood of the sin offering were treated with extreme reverence. If blood accidentally splashed onto a garment, it had to be washed out within the sacred courtyard so holy blood was not carried out into common areas. A clay pot used to boil the meat absorbed the juices and had to be broken, while a bronze pot could be thoroughly scrubbed and rinsed. These rules taught the people that sin defiles deeply and that God's work of cleansing is completely holy.

Any male in Aaron's family was allowed to eat from the regular sin offerings of the people. However, God makes a strict exception for sacrifices whose blood was brought inside the Holy Place of the Tent, such as offerings for the high priest or the whole nation. The meat of those offerings could never be eaten by any priest, but had to be burned completely outside the camp. This showed that no priest could feed upon a sacrifice offered for his own sin.
